facts.statement: Brancasaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Berriasian stage.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous (Berriasian), ~

facts.statement: Brancasaurus had a long neck with vertebrae featuring shark-fin-shaped neural spines and a small, pointed head, resembling elasmosaurids.
facts.quote: With a long neck possessing vertebrae bearing distinctively-shaped "shark fin"-shaped neural spines, and a relatively small and pointed head, Brancasaurus is superficially similar to elasmosaurids, a group to which it was long assigned.

facts.statement: The probable subadult holotype of Brancasaurus measured 3.26 meters in length.
facts.quote: It differed, however, by its more reduced size, the probable subadult holotype measuring 3.26 m in length.

facts.statement: Since 2010, phylogenetic analyses have placed Brancasaurus within or as a close relative of the family Leptocleididae.
facts.quote: Since 2010, several phylogenetic analyses have recovered Brancasaurus as a member, or a close relative, of the Leptocleididae.

facts.statement: Fossil remains of Brancasaurus come from deposits that likely represented a large continental freshwater lake.
facts.quote: Fossil remains of Brancasaurus originates from deposits who likely represented a large continental freshwater lake.

facts.statement: Workers discovered the holotype in July 1910 using pickaxes, damaging the pubis into 176 pieces, which were later collected and described by Theodor Wegner in 1914.
facts.quote: It was discovered in July 1910 by workers in the clay pit, who dug it out using pickaxes; in doing so, they damaged the specimen (in particular, the pubis had been broken into 176 pieces), and left behind a number of small fragments that were later personally collected by paleontologist Theodor Wegner, who in 1914 described the specimen in detail.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is stored at the University of Münster with the number GPMM A3.B4.
facts.quote: The described specimen is since stored at the University of Münster, where it is numbered as GPMM A3.B4.

facts.statement: The holotype is a fairly complete subadult skeleton including skull parts, most vertebrae, ribs, gastralia, girdle parts, both humeri, one femur, and flipper foot bones.
facts.quote: It is a fairly complete subadult skeleton, consisting of various parts of the skull, most of the vertebrae, several isolated ribs and gastralia, parts of the pectoral and pelvic girdles, both humeri, one femur, and various foot bones from the flippers.

facts.statement: The type specimen originates from the Isterberg Formation in the Bückeberg Group, formerly known as the German Wealden facies.
facts.quote: The clay pit from which the type specimen originates is part of the Isterberg Formation in the Bückeberg Group, also known in the past as the "German Wealden facies".

facts.statement: A cervical centrum from the Purbeck Group in southern England has a morphology comparable to Brancasaurus, suggesting the taxon may have occurred outside Germany.
facts.quote: Sachs and colleagues also noted that a cervical centra from Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary strata of the Purbeck Group in southern England exhibits a morphology comparable to that of B. brancai, suggesting that the taxon may have occurred outside Germany.

facts.statement: In 1887, Ernst Koken described two species of Plesiosaurus based on fragmentary remains found in Lower Saxony.
facts.quote: In a 1887 paper, the German paleontologist Ernst Koken described two species of Plesiosaurus, P. degenhardti and P. limnophilus, based on more or less fragmentary remains discovered in Lower Saxony.

facts.statement: Researchers found the specimen designated as Gronausaurus was virtually indistinguishable from Brancasaurus, supporting Gronausaurus as a junior synonym.
facts.quote: Sachs et al. found that this specimen, which was mature, was virtually indistinguishable from the type of Brancasaurus with the exception of the length of the ischium, the height of the cervical neural spines, the width of the cervical centra, and whether the dorsal neural spines are constricted at their base.

facts.statement: Brancasaurus was a medium-sized plesiosaur, with the holotype measuring 3.26 meters and likely belonging to a subadult.
facts.quote: Brancasaurus was a medium-sized plesiosaur, with the holotype specimen measuring 3.26 m in length; this specimen likely belongs to a subadult, judging by the unfused sutures in the vertebrae as well as the development of processes on the limbs and pubis.

facts.statement: The holotype skull of Brancasaurus is 23.7 cm long and features a snout sloping at a 15° angle.
facts.quote: The skull of the holotype, which measures 23.7 cm long, is long and narrow, with a tapered snout that slopes downwards at an angle of 15°.

facts.statement: The frontal bones of Brancasaurus form a rectangular bar separating the eye sockets.
facts.quote: The frontal bones form a rectangular bar that separates the eye sockets down the middle.

facts.statement: Ridges on the Brancasaurus skull intersect to form a dagger-shaped protrusion.
facts.quote: A ridge running across the bar intersects with the forward-extending ridge to produce a dagger-shaped protrusion.

facts.statement: It is impossible to verify if Brancasaurus had reduced tooth sockets in the premaxilla due to skull damage.
facts.quote: Although it has been suggested that Brancasaurus had very reduced tooth sockets in the premaxilla, as in Leptocleidus, this is impossible to verify because of damage to this portion of the skull.

facts.statement: The neck of Brancasaurus contains 37 vertebrae and measures approximately 1.18 meters in length.
facts.quote: The entire neck bears 37 cervical vertebrae, and is approximately 1.18 m long.

facts.statement: The neural spines of Brancasaurus vertebrae are high and triangular, resembling shark fins.
facts.quote: The neural spines of the vertebrae are distinctively shaped like shark fins, being high and triangular.

facts.statement: Brancasaurus has three pectoral vertebrae with rectangular neural spines directed slightly backwards.
facts.quote: There are three pectoral vertebrae at the neck-body transition, which are weakly concave, taller than they are long, and have rectangular-shaped neural spines that are directed slightly backwards.

facts.statement: The humeri of Brancasaurus are about 24 cm long and oval in cross-section.
facts.quote: The humeri, which have a length of about 24 cm, are oval in cross-section, and about half as wide as they are long at the widest point.

facts.statement: The available femur of Brancasaurus is 21.5 cm long with one concave edge and one edge that curves sharply near the bottom.
facts.quote: The only femur that is presently available is 21.5 cm long; it is concave on one edge, whereas the other edge is straight near the top but curves sharply near the bottom.

facts.statement: The 14 preserved phalanges of Brancasaurus are long and hourglass-shaped.
facts.quote: The 14 preserved phalanges, which likely include elements from both the forelimbs and the hindlimbs, are long and hourglass-shaped.

facts.statement: Soft tissue was apparently preserved in the Brancasaurus specimen but was removed during preparation.
facts.quote: Soft tissue was apparently preserved with the specimen, but was subsequently removed during preparation.

facts.statement: Sediment in the abdominal region of Brancasaurus may have represented gut contents including gastroliths and digested bones.
facts.quote: Additionally, an accumulation of sediment in the abdominal region may have represented gut contents, with both gastroliths and digested bones.

facts.statement: Brancasaurus is known from an almost complete fossil specimen found near Gronau in northwestern Germany.
facts.quote: Este reptil es conocido gracias al fósil casi completo de un espécimen encontrado cerca de Gronau_(Borken), en el noroeste de Alemania.

facts.statement: Brancasaurus was modest in size compared to many other plesiosaurs, reaching no more than 3.5 meters in length.
facts.quote: Su longitud es más modesta comparada con la de muchos otros plesiosaurios (por ejemplo, Elasmosaurus), y no sobrepasaba los 3,5 metros.

facts.statement: Like other plesiosaurs, Brancasaurus had limbs modified into flippers, a long neck, and a small head armed with sharp teeth.
facts.quote: Como todos los plesiosaurios, también Brancasaurus tenía sus miembros transformados en aletas, un cuello largo y una cabeza pequeña armada con dientes afilados.

facts.statement: Brancasaurus is an extinct genus of leptocleidid plesiosaur from the Early Cretaceous of what is now Germany.
facts.quote: Brancasaurus es un género extinto de plesiosaurio leptocleídido del Cretácico inferior de lo que hoy es Alemania.

facts.statement: Brancasaurus lived during the Berriasian stage, between 139.1 and 137.05 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Berriasian to Berriasian (139.1 to 137.05 million years ago)

facts.statement: Brancasaurus originated from the Bückeberg Group, which likely represented a large continental freshwater lake.
facts.quote: The Bückeberg Group, from which Brancasaurus originates, likely represented a large, continental freshwater lake that the surrounding uplands drained into.

facts.statement: During the deposition of the Wealden 5 and Wealden 6 layers, the lake expanded and became more brackish due to marine transgression.
facts.quote: During the time at which the layers of "Wealden 5" and "Wealden 6" were deposited, the lake expanded and became more brackish as a result of marine transgression.

facts.statement: Brancasaurus likely preyed on ray-finned fish such as Caturus, Lepidotes, Coelodus, Ionoscopus, and Ainia in surface waters.
facts.quote: the actinopterygian fish Caturus, Lepidotes, Coelodus, Ionoscopus, and Ainia, which Brancasaurus would have preyed on in surface waters

facts.statement: The type species is Brancasaurus brancai, named by Wegner in 1914 in honor of the German paleontologist Wilhelm von Branca.
facts.quote: La especie tipo es Brancasaurus brancai, en primer lugar el nombre de Wegner en 1914 en honor del paleontólogo alemán Wilhelm von Branca.

facts.statement: Brancasaurus was originally described in 1914 and was long considered one of the most basal members of the elasmosaurid family.
facts.quote: Brancasaurus fue descrito originalmente en 1914 y fue durante mucho tiempo considerado como uno de los miembros más basales ("primitivos") de la familia de los elasmosáuridos

facts.statement: A more recent study by Ketchum and Benson in 2010 assigned Brancasaurus to the family Leptocleididae.
facts.quote: Uno estudio más reciente (Ketchum & Benson, 2010) ha asignado a Brancasaurus en la familia de los leptocleididos

facts.statement: The parent group of Brancasaurus is the family Leptocleididae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Leptocleididae

facts.statement: Plesiosaurs of the Bückeberg Group, including Brancasaurus, were presumably preserved after sinking to the oxygen-poor bottom of the lake.
facts.quote: The deposited sediments probably represent the oxygen-poor bottom portion of the lake, with the plesiosaurs of the Bückeberg Group being presumably preserved after they sank through the water column to the bottom.

rejected.statement: The only known species, B. brancai, was first described in 1914 from a skeleton found near Gronau, North Rhine-Westphalia, in 1910.
rejected.quote: The only known species is B. brancai, first described in 1914 from a relatively complete fossil skeleton discovered four years earlier near Gronau, North Rhine-Westphalia.

rejected.statement: In 2013, Oliver Hampe designated a second fragmentary skeleton as the holotype of the new genus and species Gronausaurus wegneri.
rejected.quote: In 2013, the German paleontologist Oliver Hampe designated a second, more fragmentary skeleton as the holotype of a new genus and species, Gronausaurus wegneri.

rejected.quote: The comparatively smaller first sacral rib is directed further outwards and backwards than the other two ribs.

rejected.quote: A 2016 phylogenetic analysis conducted by Sachs et al. found two equally strong alternative placements of Brancasaurus (including Gronausaurus): within the Leptocleididae; or as the sister taxon of a clade containing both Leptocleididae and Polycotylidae, with the clade containing all of the aforementioned taxa being the sister taxon of Elasmosauridae.
